about: Every fact the game teaches, with where it came from. status: verified = the source page was read and says this; sourced = a source is recorded but the wording or figure still needs a read of the page; needs-review = not good enough to ship. tools/check-facts.mjs fails when a shipped fact has no row or no https source, and with --release also fails on anything that is not verified. A note records anything the source left unclear and any figure corrected on the second read.

facts.claim: The hood (burqa) is the falconer's main tool; it calms the falcon by limiting what it can see.
Falconers in the UAE now train falcons with drones that carry the lure; before, a lure was hung under a kite or balloon.
In the season falcons are trained twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, to avoid the heat.
Arab falconers carry the falcon on a cuff called the mangalah, which can be covered with carpet or canvas, instead of a glove.
The falcon's block perch is called the wakr; the falcon rests on it before and after the hunt.
Abu Dhabi's 2026-27 falconry season runs from 20 October 2026 to 15 February 2027.
A falconry hunting licence in Abu Dhabi costs Dh127 per season, is for one season only and must be carried while hunting.
Licensed falconry is allowed only in open desert, at least 2 km from roads, between sunrise and sunset.
Hunting wild animals and birds is banned; licensed falconers may hunt captive-bred houbara only.
Al Marzoom reserve in Al Dhafra is about 200 square km; hunting there is with falcons and salukis only, no firearms.
The UAE introduced falcon passports in 2002 to stop smuggling; more than 28,000 had been issued by 2013.
The falcon passport is valid for three years and requires a closed leg ring, which marks a captive-bred bird.
Bedouin have flown falcons since before Islam; the game they caught added to the family's food in the desert.
In the past a falcon was kept for only three or four months and released before summer; today birds are captive-bred and kept for years.
The falcon's hood is an Arab invention that reached Europe in the Middle Ages.
UNESCO announced the registration of falconry as living human heritage in November 2010 (committee meeting in Nairobi), in a multinational file whose efforts were led and coordinated by the UAE.
facts.note: The article is dated 17 Nov 2010. It is inconsistent about the count (it lists 11 countries including the UAE, and elsewhere says twelve), so the card gives no number.

facts.claim: The UNESCO file 'Falconry, a living human heritage' (no. 01708) lists 24 States Parties, the United Arab Emirates among them.
facts.note: The 24 countries were counted from the page's own list. The card gives no year.

facts.claim: UNESCO's description of the element says falconry has been practised for over 4000 years.
facts.note: Read verbatim in the Committee's decision 16.COM 8.b.14.

facts.claim: Abu Dhabi hosted the first international conference on falconry and conservation in 1976, under Sheikh Zayed.
facts.note: Gulf News names it the International Conference on Falconry and Nature Conservation, 'late 1976'.

facts.claim: The Sheikh Zayed Falcon Release Programme was established in 1995 and had returned 2,355 saker and peregrine falcons to the wild by its May 2025 release in Kazakhstan.
facts.note: The card says 'more than 2,300'. An earlier draft said 'more than 2,400' from a WAM page that could not be read; corrected.

facts.claim: A census counted more than 5,000 Emirati falconers.

The Mohamed bin Zayed Falconry and Desert Physiognomy School officially opened in December 2016 and is based at Telal Resort in Al Ain; it is described as the first institution in the world to teach Arab falconry traditions.
facts.note: December 2016 and Telal Resort are from the Khaleej Times article; 'Remah' is not on either page and was removed from the card.

facts.claim: The falconry school celebrated the graduation of its first group of women falconers, reported on 14 January 2018.
facts.note: The year is the article's publication date.

facts.claim: The saluki hound finds and flushes game for the falcon.
A houbara escapes by running or flying low, and spirals upward when chased to spoil the falcon's dive.
The International Fund for Houbara Conservation breeds about 90,000 to 100,000 houbara a year.
The Asian houbara is listed as Vulnerable.
Aspergillosis, a fungal lung disease, is described as the most important disease of falcons in the Middle East.
A 2024 study of 3,754 young falcons in the UAE found pure gyrfalcons had aspergillosis more often than gyr hybrids.
Heavy falcons such as gyrs get bumblefoot, a foot infection, when the perch material is wrong.
A GPS tracker for a falcon costs about Dh7,000 and is treated as essential equipment.
Gulf falconers traditionally preferred the saker, seen as strong and less likely to be hurt when taking houbara.
The male peregrine, the tiercel, is about a third smaller than the female.
In the Fazza Championships for Falconry the final races are over 400 metres in a straight line; a trainer reported 16.4 seconds for a farakh and 16.5 for a jirnas.
facts.note: Article of March 2015. An earlier draft said 17 to 18 seconds; corrected.

facts.claim: Racing falcons are separated into farakh (under one year of age) and jirnas (over one year), each with races for saker and shaheen (peregrine).
Falcons breed once a year in spring, triggered by the longer days; breeders add light to lengthen the day.
A gyrfalcon lays 1 to 5 eggs and incubates them for 34 to 36 days.
If the first clutch is taken to an incubator, the falcon can lay a second clutch.
A 'Gyr Pure Ultra White' falcon sold for Dh2.1 million at the final falcon auction of ADIHEX 2026 in Abu Dhabi; organisers said it was the highest price ever paid for a falcon at auction.
facts.note: Published 7 Sept 2026. The record claim is the organisers'.

held_back.claim: Abu Dhabi Falcon Hospital opened in 1999 and treats about 11,000 falcons a year.
held_back.why: only an encyclopedia page was found; needs the hospital's own figures

held_back.claim: A peregrine stoops at 250 to 300 km/h.
held_back.why: source was a general Arabic encyclopedia site

held_back.claim: Broken feathers are mended by imping.
held_back.why: source was a travel magazine; procedure details unverified
